stages.label: Smooth purees
stages.description: Very smooth, strained or pureed foods, thinned with breast milk, formula or water.

stages.label: Thicker purees and mashed
stages.description: Thicker purees and soft foods mashed with a fork, a little less smooth each week.

stages.label: Lumpy and soft finger foods
stages.description: Mashed and lumpy textures, plus soft finger foods your baby can pick up.

stages.label: Finely chopped
stages.description: Finely chopped or ground foods and a wide range of soft finger foods.

stages.label: Chopped family foods
stages.description: Soft, chopped versions of family meals, cut into pieces no bigger than about 1/2 inch.

weeks.title: First tastes
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Start with a teaspoon or two of one smooth, single-ingredient food, once a day, at a calm time. Half a spoonful is plenty at first.
Some babies do better with a little breast milk or formula first, then a few tastes, then more milk. Breast milk or formula is still the main nutrition.
tryFoods: Iron-fortified oat or barley infant cereal
tips: Thin cereal with breast milk, formula or water, and serve it from a spoon. Never put cereal in a bottle.
If your baby turns away or cries, stop and try again another day.

weeks.title: Iron-rich foods
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] From about 6 months, your baby needs iron and zinc from food. Meat, poultry, eggs and fish have the type of iron the body absorbs most easily.
Plant sources like iron-fortified cereal, beans, lentils and tofu are absorbed better alongside vitamin C foods such as sweet potatoes, broccoli, berries or tomatoes.
tips: Remove fat, skin and bones before cooking meat, then puree it until very smooth.
Wait 3 to 5 days between new foods so you can spot any reaction.

weeks.title: Hungry or full?
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Your baby will tell you how much they want. Opening their mouth, reaching or getting excited means "more"; closing their mouth, turning away or pushing food away means "done."
Let your baby decide how much to eat. They don't need to finish the bowl, and food works best when it isn't used as a reward.

allergen.label: Egg
allergen.howTo: A small taste of well-cooked egg, mashed or thinned (hard-boiled or scrambled until fully set).

tips: Offer the egg on its own day, so it's the only new food.
Once egg is tolerated, keep it in the diet regularly.

weeks.title: Peanut, the early way
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Offering peanut early, then regularly, can help prevent peanut allergy. Studies found this protection lasted.
If your baby has severe, persistent eczema or has had an allergic reaction to a food such as egg, talk to your pediatrician before offering peanut.

allergen.label: Peanut
allergen.howTo: A small amount of smooth peanut butter thinned into cereal, fruit puree or yogurt, or dissolved in breast milk or formula. Never whole peanuts.

tips: Peanut butter is only safe thinned. Chunks or spoonfuls are a choking hazard.
Keep offering egg. A typical portion is about 1/3 of a well-cooked egg.

weeks.title: Thicker textures
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] As your baby gets the hang of swallowing, make purees a little thicker and start mashing soft foods with a fork.
Coughing, sputtering and gagging are a normal part of learning new textures. Stay calm and keep your baby sitting upright.

allergen.label: Dairy
allergen.howTo: Plain whole-milk yogurt with no added sugar. (Cow's milk as a drink waits until 12 months.)

tips: Yogurt and cheese are fine before 12 months, but cow's milk as a drink waits until then.
Choose pasteurized dairy with no added sugar.

weeks.title: A first cup
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Now is a good time to offer a little water in an open cup, a cup with a spouted lid or a cup with a straw. From 6 to 12 months, 4 to 8 oz of water a day is plenty.
Breast milk or formula still provides most of what your baby drinks. Juice isn't recommended before 12 months.

allergen.label: Wheat
allergen.howTo: Infant cereal that contains wheat, or very soft, well-cooked pasta mashed small.

tips: Expect spills. Practice matters more than how much goes in.
Infant cereal is one easy way to offer wheat; check the label.

weeks.title: Try, try again
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] It's normal for a baby to refuse a new food. Many children need 8 to 10 tries before they accept it.
If a food is refused, wait about a week and offer it again, or mix it with a food your baby already likes.
tips: Freezing small portions (for up to 3 months) makes repeat tries easy and cuts waste.
Eat the food yourself first; babies learn by watching.

weeks.title: A rainbow of foods
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] By 7 or 8 months, many babies are eating foods from every food group: vegetables, fruits, proteins, dairy without added sugar, and whole grains.
Aim for different colors across the week. If you serve infant cereal, rotate oat, barley and multigrain rather than only rice cereal, which can raise arsenic exposure.

allergen.label: Sesame
allergen.howTo: A little tahini (sesame paste) thinned into a puree or yogurt.

tips: Thin tahini well, just like nut butters.
Keep offering the allergens your baby already tolerates.

weeks.title: Finger foods
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Once your baby sits up and brings things to their mouth, they can start feeding themselves soft finger foods. This builds the fine motor skills for pinching and picking up.
Good first finger foods are soft, easy to swallow and cut small: well-cooked pasta, small pieces of soft bread, ripe banana, or soft-cooked vegetables.

allergen.label: Fish
allergen.howTo: Flaked, boneless, well-cooked low-mercury fish such as salmon or cod, mashed.

tips: Choose fish low in mercury, such as salmon or cod. Remove every bone.
Always stay with your baby while they eat.

weeks.title: What's in the diaper
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Expect changes once solids begin: firmer, more colorful and stronger-smelling poop. Peas can turn it green, beets can turn it red, and small undigested bits are normal.
If poop is very loose, watery or full of mucus, slow down on solids. If it continues, call your pediatrician.

allergen.label: Shellfish
allergen.howTo: Well-cooked shrimp, very finely minced or blended into a puree.

tips: Cook shellfish thoroughly and mince it very finely.
Stop any new food that seems to cause a rash, vomiting or diarrhea, and call your pediatrician.

weeks.title: Lumpier and messier
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Move from smooth to mashed and lumpy textures as your baby's chewing improves. Around 9 months, babies can start learning to drink from a cup without a lid.
A meal for a baby this age is often around 4 oz of food, about one small jar of baby food, but appetite varies from day to day.

allergen.label: Tree nuts
allergen.howTo: A smooth tree-nut butter (such as almond or cashew) thinned into a puree. Never whole nuts.

tips: Use a smooth nut butter, thinned. Whole or chopped nuts are a choking hazard.
Let your baby touch and squish food. Mess is part of learning.

weeks.title: Keep allergens on the menu
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] If your baby has now tried all nine common allergens, the next step is keeping them in the diet regularly, in portions suited to your baby.
Check the allergen tracker. If any are still untried, or a reaction was logged, talk to your pediatrician about what to do next.
tryFoods: Small, thin slices of pasteurized mild cheese
tips: Typical portions: about 1 teaspoon of a thinned nut or seed butter, or about 1/3 of a well-cooked egg.
Cut cheese into short, thin strips, never chunks.

weeks.title: Finely chopped
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Your baby can begin eating finely chopped or ground foods as their skills grow. Keep pieces small and soft enough to mash between your fingers.
Whole grain kernels such as barley, wheat berries or brown rice should be cooked and finely ground or mashed.
tips: Cut round foods like blueberries and grapes into small pieces.
Keep watching for reactions whenever you add something new.

weeks.title: A daily rhythm
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Most babies this age eat something every 2 to 3 hours: about 3 meals and 2 to 3 snacks a day, alongside breast milk or formula.
Regular meal and snack times help. Try not to let your baby graze or sip all day long.
tips: Plan snacks as mini-meals: a fruit or vegetable plus a protein or grain.
If you're worried about how much your baby eats, talk to your pediatrician.

weeks.title: Eating together
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Family meals can start from the very first feeding. Babies learn to eat by watching you eat and enjoy food.
When you can, sit together, keep the TV off and the mood calm, and let your baby join in.
tryFoods: Mashed beans on soft toast fingers
tips: Set aside your baby's portion before adding salt, sugar or spicy seasoning.
Keep mealtimes unhurried; rushing raises the risk of choking.

weeks.title: Iron check-in
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Iron supports your baby's brain development and growth. Include an iron-rich food most days: meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans, lentils, tofu or iron-fortified cereal.
Babies born early may need extra iron. Your pediatrician will likely check for anemia around 12 months.
tips: Pair plant iron with vitamin C: beans with tomatoes, or cereal with berries.
Ask your pediatrician if you have questions about iron drops or supplements.

weeks.title: No added salt or sugar
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Babies and toddlers have no room in their diet for added sugars. Skip sweetened yogurts, cookies and sweet drinks.
Go easy on salt too. Choose canned foods labeled low sodium or no salt added, and limit processed foods made for adults.
tips: Read the Nutrition Facts label for added sugars and sodium.
No honey before 12 months: it can cause infant botulism, a severe food poisoning.

weeks.title: Self-feeding
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Between about 10 and 12 months, babies start trying to use a spoon themselves. Give them a chance, even though it's messy.
Offer soft finger foods at each meal too. By 12 months, most babies can easily feed themselves with their fingers.
tips: Pinching small, soft pieces builds fine motor skills.
Let your baby practice with a spoon or fork, even when it's messy.

weeks.title: Family foods, chopped
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Your baby can now eat many of the foods you eat, made soft and chopped into pieces no bigger than about 1/2 inch.
Choose family meals built around vegetables, fruits, proteins, whole grains and dairy, and adapt the texture for your baby.
tips: Serve your baby's portion before adding salt or hot spices.
Keep food soft enough to mash with a fork.

weeks.title: Choking-safe shapes
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Shape matters as much as texture. Cut round foods like grapes, cherries and cherry tomatoes into small pieces, and cut long foods like hot dogs, sausages and string cheese into short, thin strips.
Avoid popcorn, nuts, hard candy, chips, and raw hard fruits or vegetables. Your baby should always eat sitting upright and supervised.
tips: Ask your pediatrician what to do if your baby chokes.
No eating in the car, in the stroller or while crawling.

weeks.title: Fish for growing brains
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Fish provides nutrients that support brain development, plus iron and zinc. Choose fish from the FDA's "Best Choices" list, such as salmon, cod, tilapia or canned light tuna.
Around age 1, a child-size serving is about 1 oz. Avoid high-mercury fish like shark, swordfish and king mackerel.
tips: Check carefully for bones, even in fillets.
Fish also provides protein, vitamin B12, vitamin D and selenium.

weeks.title: Let them lead
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Your baby's appetite can change a lot from meal to meal and day to day. This is normal.
Keep offering a variety of healthy foods, and let your baby decide whether and how much to eat. Talk to your pediatrician if you're worried about growth.
tryFoods: Whole grain pasta with soft vegetables
tips: Pushing food away or turning their head means "done."
Avoid using food as a reward or punishment.

weeks.title: Safe food handling
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Homemade baby food spoils faster than jarred. Refrigerate leftovers promptly, use them within 1 day, and check for signs of spoilage before serving.
Serve only pasteurized milk products and juices. Raw milk and unpasteurized cheeses can carry harmful bacteria.
tips: Freeze extra purees in small portions and use them within 3 months.
Choose cheeses and yogurts labeled pasteurized.

weeks.title: Picky phases
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Babies sometimes refuse foods they used to love. Liking only a few foods, or not wanting foods to touch, are normal phases.
Keep foods your baby likes on the plate alongside something new, and give simple choices so they feel in control.
tips: Make it playful: a smiley face on the plate can help.
Model eating the food yourself.

weeks.title: Getting ready for 12 months
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] At 12 months, and not before, you can start offering plain, pasteurized whole cow's milk or a fortified, unsweetened dairy alternative in a cup.
Milk is a drink, not a replacement for food. Juice isn't needed. If you offer it after 12 months, keep it to 100% juice, no more than 4 oz a day, in a cup.
tips: Talk to your pediatrician about moving from formula or bottles.
No honey until your baby's first birthday.

weeks.title: First birthday
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Around 12 months, growth slows down and many children eat less than before. Some days they'll hardly eat; over a week, they usually get what they need.
Your baby will likely have a checkup around now, including an anemia test. Bring your questions about food, milk and the next stage.
tryFoods: Soft-cooked pasta with tomato sauce (no added salt)
tips: Keep offering all the allergens your baby tolerates.
The monthly guides on the Today tab keep going into the toddler years.

readiness.intro: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Most babies are ready for solid foods at about 6 months. Starting before 4 months isn't recommended. Look for these signs together:
signs: Sits up alone or with support
Opens their mouth when food comes their way
Swallows food rather than pushing it out onto their chin
Tries to grasp small objects, like toys or food

choking.intro: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Choking is silent and serious. Gagging (coughing, sputtering, pushing food forward) is a normal part of learning to eat. Know the difference, and consider an infant CPR and first-aid class.
signs: Can't breathe, cry or make a sound

groups.title: At every meal
items: Always watch your child while they eat.
Sit them upright in a high chair or safe seat; no eating while lying down, crawling, walking, or in the car or stroller.
Serve foods with the right texture for their stage.

groups.title: 6 to 12 months: avoid or change
items: Whole or chopped nuts and seeds; chunks or spoonfuls of nut or seed butter (thin it instead).
Uncut grapes, cherries, berries, cherry tomatoes and melon balls (cut into small pieces).
Raw hard vegetables or fruit like carrots and apples (cook until soft); whole pieces of canned fruit.
Hot dogs, sausages and meat sticks; tough or large chunks of meat; bones in meat or fish.
Large chunks of cheese, especially string cheese (cut into short, thin strips).
Whole corn kernels, whole beans, and raisins or other dried fruit.
Popcorn, chips, pretzels, cookies and granola bars; crackers or bread with seeds, nut pieces or whole grain kernels.
Whole kernels of cooked barley, wheat or other grains (grind or mash them).
Hard, round or sticky candy, gummies, marshmallows and gum.

groups.title: 1 to 4 years: still take care
items: Children don't chew with a grinding motion until about age 4.
Cut food into pieces no larger than about 1/2 inch.
Quarter grapes and cherry tomatoes; cut hot dogs lengthwise, then into small pieces.
Spread nut butter thinly on bread or a cracker; never by the spoonful.
Keep high-risk foods like whole nuts, popcorn and hard candy away until about age 4 or later.
